7	1. Overview
8	
9	AIRcoin pays people for growing pollution-absorbing plants. A low-cost camera "miner"
10	watches up to 20 tagged plants and estimates the pollution they remove. It mints AIRcoin
11	as proof of that useful work. Polluting companies must buy and burn AIRcoin to meet
12	compliance, which creates demand.
13	
14	Problem. Urban air pollution (PM2.5, PM10, NO, SO, CO, VOCs, CO) has no direct,
15	verifiable incentive for citizens to fight it. Carbon credits target large projects and are
16	hard for households to join.
17	
18	Product in one line. A plant-monitoring miner, a token minted from verified plant work,
19	and a marketplace where citizens sell the token and polluters buy and burn it.
20	
21	Hackathon goal. Show a working end-to-end system on stage:
22	
23	    A physical 20-plant rig with a real camera, Raspberry Pi and GPS.
24	    A live digital twin: camera feed with detections, a 3D model of the miner's insides,
25	    sensor gauges and a minting ticker.
26	    Live anti-cheat: removing a plant, adding a fake plant or reusing a sticker is caught on
27	    screen.
28	    Real miner software fed by simulated sensor data, minting real AIRcoin on a blockchain
29	    testnet.
30	    A wallet and marketplace where an owner sells AIRcoin and a company buys and burns
31	    it for compliance.
32

76	2.2 The stickers
77	
78	Each miner ships with 20 printed fiducial stickers (ArUco or AprilTag markers). Every
79	sticker ID is registered to exactly one miner at sale time. A sticker seen by a different
80	miner, or by its own miner at a new location, is rejected. This stops owners from moving
81	the same plants between miners to mint twice.
82

179	Shreyas turns the evidence into a multiplier per species and pollutant group (High 1.5,
180	Medium 1.0, Low 0.5) on Day 1. The estimator applies these multipliers to generic base
181	rates for PM deposition, CO uptake and VOC removal.
182	
183	Pitch caveat: sealed-chamber results do not scale to real rooms. Cummings and Waring
184	(2019) estimate 100 to 1,000 plants per m� of floor would be needed to match normal
185	ventilation. AIRcoin therefore credits estimated removal per plant. It does not claim a pot
186	cleans a room, and the enclosure calibration exists to replace literature numbers with
187	measured ones.
188	
189	2.4 Calibration
190	
191	We estimate each species' uptake by placing it in a closed enclosure with known pollutant
192	levels and measuring the drop over time, per unit of leaf area. The result is a coefficient
193	table: species � pollutant  grams removed per m� of leaf per hour at a reference
194	concentration. For the hackathon this table is seeded from published literature and
195	labelled as an estimate.
196	
197	2.5 Proof of Useful Work (minting)
198	
199	1. The miner watches its plants continuously and identifies each tagged plant, its
200	    species, its visible leaf area and whether it is alive.
201	
202	2. It reads ambient air quality (local sensors plus GPS-based AQI).
203	3. Every epoch it estimates pollution removed per plant using the calibration table.
204	4. It signs an attestation: miner ID, epoch, plant states, sensor summary, GPS, image
205	
206	    hashes and the claimed amount.
207	5. A validator checks the signature, the sticker bindings, location and plausibility, then
208	
209	    mints AIRcoin to the owner's wallet.
210	
211	                                                                                                    Page 4 of 21
212	 AIRcoin -- Product Requirements Document
213	
214	Estimation model (per plant i, per pollutant p, per epoch):
215	
216	  R_{i,p} = k_{s(i),p} \times A_i \times H_i \times f\left(\frac{C_p}
217	  {C_{p,\mathrm{ref}}}\right) \times \Delta t
218	
219	k = calibrated coefficient for species s, A = estimated leaf area, H = health/liveness score
220	(0 to 1), C = ambient concentration, f = a capped concentration factor, t = epoch length.
221	Pollutant amounts are weighted into one unit, defined in 2.6.
222	
223	2.6 What 1 AIR means
224	
225	1 AIR = the health damage avoided by removing 1 mg of PM2.5 (1 mg PM2.5-equivalent).
226	Other pollutants convert by their damage cost relative to PM2.5, using the central EU
227	values in CE Delft's Environmental Prices Handbook (Table 1, 2015 per kg).
228	
229	Pollutant                                 Damage cost (/kg)  Weight (PM2.5 = 1)
230	PM2.5                                     38.7               1.00
231	PM10                                      26.6               0.69
232	NO (NO)                                   14.8               0.38
233	SO                                        11.5               0.30
234	VOCs (benzene, formaldehyde and others)   1.15               0.030
235	CO                                        0.057              0.0015
236	CO                                        0.0526             0.0014
237	
238	  \mathrm{AIR}_{\mathrm{epoch}} = \sum_{p} w_p \times \sum_{i} R_{i,p}\,
239	  [\mathrm{mg}]
240	
241	Why this unit: it rewards the pollutants that harm health most, it puts CO and toxic gases
242	on one scale, and milligrams give readable numbers on screen. A full 20-plant miner
243	should earn on the order of tens of AIR per day, mostly from CO uptake and dust capture;
244	Shreyas confirms the figure from the calibration table on Day 1. The EU prices are a stand-
245	in; India-specific damage costs can replace them later without changing the unit.
246	
247	2.7 Marketplace and demand
248	
249	    Citizens apply on the platform to buy a miner. A government admin reviews and
250	    approves each application; approval registers the miner and its 20 stickers on-chain.
251	    Owners sell AIRcoin on our marketplace for rupee-pegged test stablecoin.
252	
253	                                                             Page 5 of 21
254	 AIRcoin -- Product Requirements Document
255	
256	The regulator assigns each polluting company a yearly AIRcoin burn obligation.
257	Because factories emit tonnes and plants remove milligrams, the obligation is a set
258	share of each company's weighted emissions, not a full offset.
259	
260	Companies buy AIRcoin and burn it through a compliance function that records which
261	obligation it meets.
262	
263	Burning permanently removes supply, so steady obligations create steady demand.
264	
265	The government admin monitors the whole platform: every miner's live sensors and
266	status, mints, trades, burns and flagged proofs. The government can later run the
267	validator and registry itself.

481	7. Workstream A � Vision and digital twin (Omkar)
482	
483	Mission: make the miner see. Detect every tagged plant, prove it is the right species and
484	alive, and show all of it live in a digital twin judges can explore.
485	
486	                                                                                                Page 11 of 21
487	 AIRcoin -- Product Requirements Document
488	
489	Stack: Raspberry Pi 4/5, Pi Camera Module 3 NoIR Wide with a blue gel filter, Python,
490	OpenCV ( cv2.aruco ), a pretrained MobileNetV3 for plant-match embeddings (no
491	training), React + Vite, react-three-fiber (Three.js), Blender  glTF, Leaflet for the map,
492	MQTT over WebSockets.
493	
494	7.1 Components
495	
496	 1. Physical rig. A board with 20 pot slots in a 4 � 5 grid, camera on a fixed mount 1 to 1.5 m
497	    away so all 20 stickers are readable in one frame. One plastic plant and one spare
498	    sticker kept aside for the anti-cheat demo.
499	
500	 2. Stickers. ArUco markers (4�4 or 5�5 dictionary), IDs 0-19 for this miner, printed 4-5
501	    cm on waterproof labels and fixed to a stake at the plant's base. Known marker size
502	    doubles as a scale reference for measuring plant size.
503	
504	 3. Tag detection. Detect and decode all markers each frame; match IDs against the
505	    miner's registered sticker set. Unknown IDs are flagged.
506	
507	 4. Plant match. At setup, photograph each tagged plant and store a feature vector from a
508	    pretrained network. Each cycle, compare the live crop above the tag with that stored
509	    vector; a low match means the plant was swapped and is flagged. This replaces a 20-
510	    species classifier, which can't be trained well in three days.
511	
512	 5. Plant size. Segment green pixels in the crop (HSV threshold or excess-green index),
513	    convert to cm� using the marker's known size. Smooth over time.
514	
515	 6. Liveness (fake-plant check). Primary: NDVI from the NoIR camera with a blue filter
516	    (living leaves reflect near-infrared; plastic does not). Fallback: a low plant-match score
517	    plus texture and colour variance. Output alive_score 0-1.
518	
519	 7. Status machine. Per tag: present  missing after 10 s unseen  removed after 60 s;
520	    suspect when species mismatches or alive_score is low. Debounced so a hand
521	    passing in front doesn't trigger alerts.
522	
523	 8. Live feed. Annotated stream (boxes, tag IDs, species, status colour) at about 15 fps,
524	    720p, via MJPEG or WebRTC. The NoIR camera shows false colours, so the twin offers
525	    two views: the raw feed and an NDVI heat map where living leaves glow. Inference runs
526	    at 1-2 Hz.
527	
528	 9. Digital twin web app.
529	        3D miner model built in Blender: case, Raspberry Pi, camera, GPS module, sensor
530	        boards, wiring. Exploded view on click; each part shows its live reading.
531	        Virtual 20-slot plant grid mirroring the rig: green = healthy, grey = missing, red =
532	        suspect.
533	        Live camera panel, sensor gauges and AQI chart (from C2), mint ticker and wallet
534	        balance (from C4), anti-cheat event log, GPS pin on a map.

583	8.1 Components
584	
585	 1. Sensor layer. One driver interface per sensor (PM, gas/VOC, CO, NO,
586	     temp/humidity). All air sensors are simulated for the hackathon; only the camera and
587	     GPS are real. Real PMS5003, MQ-135, SCD40 and BME280 drivers can drop in later
588	     without other code changing. Optional: if a DHT22 or BME280 is already on hand, wire
589	     it so one reading in the twin is live.
590	
591	 2. Sensor simulator. Daily curves plus noise, with correlated values (PM10 tracks PM2.5,
592	     humidity affects PM). Named scenarios: clean morning (AQI about 50), rush hour
593	     (about 180), festival smog (about 400), rain washout. Switchable live.
594	
595	 3. GPS service. Reads the real GPS module; falls back to a fixed demo location indoors
596	     where there's no fix. Reports location and fix quality.
597	
598	 4. Vision subscriber. Consumes C1 and keeps the latest state of each of the 20 plants.
599	 5. Species catalogue and calibration table. 20 species � pollutants coefficient table,
600	
601	     seeded from published studies, versioned; its hash goes into every attestation. The
602	     species list is fixed in 2.3; B sets the multipliers.
603	 6. Estimation engine. Applies the model in section 2.5 per plant per epoch. Caps per
604	     plant and per epoch. Missing plants count zero; suspect plants count zero and raise a
605	     flag.
606	 7. Epoch manager. Epoch = 60 s in real time for the demo (no time acceleration), 1 hour in
607	     production.
608	 8. Attestation signer. Builds the C3 payload, hashes the evidence (frame hashes + sensor
609	     readings + plant states + GPS), signs with the device key. Keys generated on first boot
610	     and registered with C's registry.
611	 9. Uplink. Posts C3 with retry and an offline queue so no epoch is lost if Wi-Fi drops.
612	10. Telemetry. Publishes C2 every second and every epoch.
613	11. Device-side anti-cheat flags. Unknown sticker, species mismatch, low liveness, GPS
614	     more than 50 m from the registered spot, frozen camera (identical frame hashes), too
615	     many plants appearing at once, clock drift.
616	12. Scenario controller. A web panel for the demo: change AQI scenario, simulate moving
617	     the miner, reset.
618	13. Calibration protocol (document). How the real enclosure test would work: sealed box,
619	     reference sensor, controlled pollutant source, decay measured with and without each
620	     species, coefficients fitted per m� of leaf. Used in the pitch to answer "how do you
621	     know?"
